intro: Watch a skater ollie and the board seems to jump up and stick to the shoes. Nothing is glued. In about half a second, a stomp on the tail, a lever, a push back from the ground, a dragging shoe, the pull of gravity and a soft landing all work together. Each of those has a name in physics, and each can be measured with a ruler, a phone camera and a calculator.

This unit takes the ollie apart one piece at a time. You will see the board as a lever that turns around its rear wheels, and work out torque in newton-meters. You will learn why the kicktail, patented in 1971, changed what skaters could do, and how Newton's third law explains the pop. Then you will follow the grip tape's friction, the order of the moves, the parabola the body traces in the air, and the arithmetic of hang time and landing.

By the end you will be able to explain each step of an ollie and the force behind it, practice the motion safely starting on grass or carpet, and work out how long a jump lasts and why bent knees make a landing gentler. Regular or goofy, first try or hundredth, the same physics is at work under every board.
bigQuestion: How do levers, friction and gravity let a skater lift a board off flat ground with no hands?

test.q: What acts as the pivot when a skater presses down on the tail?
test.why: The board turns around the rear wheels when the tail is pressed, so they are the pivot.

test.q: A 400 N stomp lands 0.12 m from the rear wheels. What torque does it make?
Why does a skater put the ball of the back foot on the end of the tail?
choices: To keep the front foot heavy
To make the board roll faster
To give the stomp the longest lever arm and most torque
test.why: The tail tip is farthest from the rear wheels, so the same stomp makes the most torque there.

test.q: What did Larry Stevenson patent in 1971?
test.why: Stevenson was granted a U.S. patent for the kicktail in 1971.

test.q: Which law of motion explains the pop, when the ground pushes back on the tail?
test.why: Newton's third law says forces come in equal, opposite pairs, so the ground pushes back up on the tail.

test.q: Why must the front foot go light at the moment of the pop?
choices: Its weight makes a torque that fights the tail's torque
It needs to push the board forward
It must hold the nose to the ground
It keeps the tail from hitting
test.why: The front foot presses on the other side of the pivot, so its torque can cancel the tail's.

test.q: In an ollie, what does friction from the grip tape do?
choices: It lets the sliding front shoe drag the board up and forward
It slows the wheels on the ground
test.why: Friction on the board points the way the shoe slides, so it pulls the board along with the foot.

test.q: Which part of an ollie comes right after the pop?
test.why: The order is crouch, pop, slide, jump, level, land.

test.q: A skater's center of mass in the air follows what kind of path?
test.why: Moving freely with gravity as the only big force, the center of mass traces a parabola.

test.q: Can a skater in the air make the center of mass go higher by tucking the knees?
choices: No, but tucking lifts the feet and board closer to it
Yes, if the arms wave too
No, because tucking stops the jump
test.why: The center of mass follows a set path, but tucking raises the feet toward it, so the board rises higher.

test.q: Using hang time = 2√(2h ÷ g), about how long does a 0.30 m rise last?
Why does a rolling skater land back on the board after an ollie?
choices: The grip tape holds the shoes
By inertia, skater and board keep the same forward speed
test.why: Newton's first law: both keep the forward speed they had before the pop.

test.q: A 50 kg skater landing at 2.4 m/s stops in 0.05 s with stiff legs. What is the extra force?
Where is the safest place to first practice the ollie motion?
choices: Standing still on grass or carpet
Rolling fast across a parking lot
On a curb next to a street
test.why: On grass or carpet the board cannot roll, so the motion can be learned before moving.

test.q: Why does a kicked tail let the nose rise higher than a flat tail?
choices: It moves the pivot to the nose
Its tip starts higher, so the board turns farther before the tail touches
test.why: A raised tip has farther to travel down, so the board turns through a bigger angle and the nose climbs higher.

write.prompt: Explain how an ollie works, step by step, to someone who has never seen one. For each of the six steps, name what the front foot and back foot do and the physics behind it. Say front foot and back foot so both regular and goofy skaters can follow.

title: The Physics of the Ollie

chapters.title: Levers and Torque
chapters.bigQuestion: How can one quick stomp on the tail lift the whole front of a skateboard into the air?

story.title: The Ruler on the Desk
story.kicker: A tapped ruler leaps off a desk, and a seventh grader sees a skateboard in it.
paragraphs: Mr. Okafor sets a wooden ruler on the edge of his desk. About a third of it sticks out past the edge. A pink eraser sits on the far end, resting on the desk. He asks the class to guess what will happen when he taps the end that hangs in the air.

He brings his finger down fast on the overhanging end. The ruler tips over the edge of the desk like a seesaw. The far end jumps up, and the eraser flies toward the ceiling. It lands in the front row, and a student named Dani catches it.

Dani turns the eraser over in her hand. She skates every weekend at the park near her house. "That is an ollie," she says. "The desk edge is like my back wheels. The part you tapped is my tail." Mr. Okafor writes two words on the board: lever and torque.

He taps the ruler again, this time close to the desk edge. The far end barely moves, and the eraser only wobbles. Then he taps the very tip of the overhang. The eraser flies higher than before. The class starts to argue about why the same tap works so differently in different places.

Dani grabs her board from her locker and sets it on the carpet. She presses the tail down slowly with her hand. The nose rises while the back wheels stay on the floor. "Same thing," she says. "Now we just need to figure out the numbers."
story.think: Why did tapping the very tip of the ruler send the eraser higher than tapping near the desk edge?

lessons.title: What a Lever Does
lessons.mainIdea: A lever is a stiff bar that turns around a fixed point, so a push on one side moves the other side.
reading: A playground seesaw is the easiest lever to picture. It is a long, stiff board resting on a bar in the middle. When one rider pushes down, the board turns around the bar, and the other rider goes up. A *lever* is any stiff bar that turns around one fixed point. Crowbars, scissors and bottle openers are levers too.

The fixed point a lever turns around is the *fulcrum*. On a seesaw the fulcrum is the bar in the middle. On Mr. Okafor's ruler it was the edge of the desk. Every part of the lever swings around the fulcrum at the same time. When one end goes down, the other end must go up.

A lever has two other parts worth naming. The *effort* is the push you put in. The load is the thing being moved, such as the eraser or the other rider. Scientists study levers because they change how a push works. A small push in the right spot can move a heavy load, or a short motion can become a long one.

words.d: a stiff bar that turns around one fixed point
the fixed point a lever turns around; also called the pivot
the push or pull a person puts into a lever

look.title: A Seesaw in Slow Motion
look.text: Picture a seesaw with a friend on each end. The bar in the middle does not move. One friend pushes off the ground and goes up. At the very same moment, the other friend sinks down. The board never bends; it just turns around the bar.
look.prompt: Point to the fulcrum, the effort and the load on this seesaw. Then find the same three parts on a pair of scissors.

check.q: What is a fulcrum?
choices: The heaviest end of a lever
The fixed point a lever turns around
The push a person gives a lever
check.why: The fulcrum is the fixed point, like the bar under a seesaw, that the lever turns around.

check.q: On Mr. Okafor's ruler, what acted as the fulcrum?
choices: The far end of the ruler
check.why: The ruler turned around the edge of the desk, so the edge was the fulcrum.

check.q: When one end of a stiff lever goes down, what does the other end do?
check.why: A stiff lever turns as one piece around the fulcrum, so the far end rises.

lessons.title: Finding the Pivot on a Board
lessons.mainIdea: When the tail is pressed down, a skateboard turns around its rear wheels, so the rear wheels are the fulcrum.
reading: Set a skateboard on a carpet or on grass, where it cannot roll away. Put your hand on the *tail*, the short end that bends up behind the back wheels. Press down slowly. The tail sinks, the back wheels stay on the floor, and the *nose* at the front lifts into the air.

The board just acted like Mr. Okafor's ruler. It turned around the place where the rear wheels touch the ground. That makes the rear wheels the fulcrum, or *pivot*, of the skateboard lever. The tail is on one side of the pivot. The rest of the board, with the front wheels and the nose, is on the other side.

This is the first thing that happens in an *ollie*, the jump where a skater and board rise together with no hands. The back foot presses the tail, the board turns around the rear wheels, and the nose comes up. Everything else in the ollie builds on this simple lever.

words.d: the back end of the deck, behind the rear wheels, usually bent upward
the front end of the deck, ahead of the front wheels
the point something turns around; on a board pressed at the tail, the rear wheels
a jump in which the skater and board leave the ground together without using hands

look.title: The Hand Test
look.text: A board rests on a carpet. A hand presses the tail down, little by little. The rear wheels stay touching the carpet the whole time. The front wheels lift off first, then the nose rises higher and higher. When the tail touches the carpet, the board stops turning.
look.prompt: Try the hand test with a real board on carpet or grass. Which wheels stay on the ground, and what stops the nose from rising any higher?

check.q: When you press the tail down, which part of the board stays on the ground and acts as the pivot?
check.why: The board turns around the rear wheels, so they stay down and act as the pivot.

check.q: Why should you test this on carpet or grass first?
choices: The board cannot roll away there
check.why: On carpet or grass the wheels do not roll, so the board stays put while you study it.

check.q: What is an ollie?
choices: Pressing the nose to spin the board
Turning on the back wheels only
A jump where skater and board rise together with no hands
check.why: An ollie is a no-hands jump in which the board rises with the skater.

lessons.title: Small Push, Big Swing
lessons.mainIdea: Points far from the pivot move farther than points close to it, so a short drop of the tail makes a big rise of the nose.
reading: Watch two dots on a turning lever. One dot is near the fulcrum, and one is far away. Both dots turn through the same angle at the same time. But the far dot travels a much longer path. On a lever, the farther a point is from the pivot, the farther it moves.

A skateboard uses this. The tail is short, and the nose is far from the rear wheels. Here is a worked example with example lengths. Say the tail tip is 0.15 m behind the rear wheels and the nose tip is 0.53 m in front of them. The nose is 0.53 ÷ 0.15, or about 3.5 times, as far from the pivot.

For small turns, each point moves in proportion to its distance from the pivot. So if the tail tip drops 5 cm, the nose tip rises about 5 × 3.5 = 17.5 cm. A short stomp at the back becomes a big lift at the front. That lift is the *ratio* of the two distances at work, and it is why the ollie starts with the tail.

words.d: how many times bigger one number is than another, found by dividing
a relationship where one amount grows by the same factor as another

look.title: Two Chalk Marks
look.text: Put one chalk mark on a board's tail tip and one on its nose tip. Press the tail until the tail mark drops the width of two fingers. Now look at the nose mark. It has climbed much higher, about three and a half times as far, because it sits about three and a half times farther from the rear wheels.
look.prompt: If the tail tip dropped 4 cm and the nose was 3.5 times as far from the pivot, about how far would the nose tip rise? Show your multiplication.

check.q: On a turning lever, which point moves farthest?
choices: The point farthest from the fulcrum
The point closest to the fulcrum
Every point moves the same distance
check.why: All points turn through the same angle, so the point farthest from the fulcrum travels the longest path.

check.q: In the worked example, the nose tip is 0.53 m from the pivot and the tail tip is 0.15 m. About how many times farther is the nose?
check.why: 0.53 ÷ 0.15 is about 3.5, so the nose is about 3.5 times as far from the pivot.

check.q: If the tail tip drops 5 cm and the ratio is 3.5, about how far does the nose tip rise?
check.why: 5 cm × 3.5 = 17.5 cm, because the nose moves in proportion to its distance from the pivot.

lessons.title: What Torque Means
lessons.mainIdea: Torque is how strongly a force turns something, and it equals the force times its distance from the pivot.
reading: Try to open a heavy door by pushing right next to the hinges. It barely moves. Push the same door near the handle, far from the hinges, and it swings open easily. The push was the same size both times. What changed was the distance between your push and the turning point.

That turning effect has a name: *torque*. Torque tells how strongly a force makes something rotate around a pivot. It depends on two things: the size of the force and how far from the pivot the force acts. That distance is called the *lever arm*. A bigger force or a longer lever arm both give more torque.

Scientists write the rule as torque = force × lever arm. Force is measured in newtons (N), and the lever arm in meters (m). So torque is measured in *newton-meters*, written N·m. A push of 20 N on a door handle 0.8 m from the hinges gives a torque of 20 × 0.8 = 16 N·m. The same push 0.1 m from the hinges gives only 20 × 0.1 = 2 N·m.

words.d: the turning effect of a force; force times its distance from the pivot
the distance from the pivot to the place where a force pushes, measured straight across
the unit of torque, written N·m: newtons of force times meters of lever arm

look.title: The Door Test
look.text: Stand at a classroom door. Push with one finger right beside the hinges. Then push with the same finger at the edge near the handle. Your finger presses about the same both times, but only the second push swings the door. The longer lever arm made more torque.
look.prompt: Try the door test gently. Then explain, using the words torque and lever arm, why door handles are put far from the hinges.

check.q: What two things does torque depend on?
choices: The color and size of the object
The force and its distance from the pivot
The speed and weight of the object
The force and the time it lasts
check.why: Torque = force × lever arm, so it depends on the force and how far from the pivot it acts.

check.q: A 20 N push acts 0.8 m from a door's hinges. What is the torque?
check.why: Torque = 20 N × 0.8 m = 16 N·m.

check.q: Why does pushing a door near the hinges barely move it?
choices: The lever arm is very short, so the torque is small
The hinges push back harder there
The door is heavier near the hinges
Force does not work near a pivot
check.why: Near the hinges the lever arm is short, so the same force makes only a small torque.

lessons.title: Tail Tip or Bolts?
lessons.mainIdea: The same stomp makes far more torque on the tip of the tail than near the rear bolts, because the lever arm is longer.
reading: A skater's back foot can stand in different places. The *bolts* are the screw heads on top of the deck that hold each truck on. The rear bolts sit just a few centimeters from the rear wheels. The tail tip is much farther back. Where the back foot presses changes how much torque it makes around the rear wheels.

Here is a worked example with example numbers. Say the back foot stomps down with 400 N, about the weight of a 41 kg person, because 41 kg × 9.8 m/s² is about 400 N. Near the bolts, the lever arm might be 0.03 m. Torque = 400 N × 0.03 m = 12 N·m. On the tail tip, the lever arm might be 0.15 m. Torque = 400 N × 0.15 m = 60 N·m.

The same foot and the same stomp give five times the torque on the tail tip, because 60 ÷ 12 = 5. That is why skaters put the ball of the back foot on the end of the tail for an ollie. A skater who stands on the rear bolts and stomps will feel the board barely tip, just like the door pushed near its hinges.

words.d: the screw heads on top of the deck that hold the trucks on; a common way to describe where to stand
the padded part of the sole just behind the toes

look.title: Same Stomp, Different Spots
look.cite: Worked example: a 400 N stomp, torque = force × lever arm
look.prompt: What happens to the torque each time the foot moves 0.03 m farther back? Why does the table go up by the same amount each row?

check.q: A 400 N stomp lands 0.15 m from the rear wheels. What torque does it make?
check.why: Torque = 400 N × 0.15 m = 60 N·m.

check.q: Where should the back foot press for the biggest torque in an ollie?
choices: On the ball of the foot at the end of the tail
In the middle of the deck
check.why: The tail tip has the longest lever arm from the rear wheels, so it gives the most torque.

check.q: Why is a stomp near the rear bolts weak for an ollie?
choices: The front wheels are too far away
The lever arm from the rear wheels is very short
The stomp is a different force there
check.why: The rear bolts are only a few centimeters from the rear wheels, so the lever arm and the torque are small.

lessons.title: Torques That Fight
lessons.mainIdea: The front foot makes a torque the other way, so it must go light at the pop or the nose will not rise.
reading: A seesaw balances when the torques on its two sides are equal. A 300 N child sitting 2 m from the middle makes 300 × 2 = 600 N·m. A 400 N child sitting 1.5 m from the middle makes 400 × 1.5 = 600 N·m. The torques are equal and opposite, so the seesaw stays level. If one side's torque gets bigger, that side goes down.

A skateboard works the same way, with the rear wheels as the middle. The back foot on the tail turns the board one way. The front foot, standing ahead of the rear wheels, turns it the other way. Say the front foot presses 200 N at a spot 0.30 m from the rear wheels, just behind the front bolts. That is 200 × 0.30 = 60 N·m against the tail.

That 60 N·m exactly cancels the 60 N·m stomp from the last lesson, and the nose would not rise at all. So in an ollie the front foot must go light at the moment the back foot snaps. The skater does this by starting to jump and lifting the front knee. The tail's torque then wins, and the nose swings up.

words.d: when the torques on both sides of a pivot are equal, so nothing turns
a torque that tries to turn something the other way

look.title: How Hard the Front Foot Presses
look.cite: Worked example: front foot 0.30 m from the rear wheels, torque = force × lever arm
look.prompt: The tail stomp makes 60 N·m. In which rows would the nose still rise? What does that tell the front foot to do?

check.q: A 400 N child sits 1.5 m from the middle of a seesaw. What torque does that child make?
check.why: Torque = 400 N × 1.5 m = 600 N·m.

check.q: Why must the front foot go light at the moment of the pop?
choices: So its torque does not cancel the tail's torque
So the back foot can slide
So the tail does not touch the ground
check.why: The front foot's torque works against the tail. If it presses hard, it cancels the tail's torque and the nose stays down.

check.q: How does a skater make the front foot light at the pop?
choices: By leaning back over the tail
By starting to jump and lifting the front knee
By pushing with the front foot
check.why: Starting the jump and lifting the front knee takes weight off the front foot, so the tail's torque wins.

lessons.title: Flat Boards Came First
lessons.mainIdea: Early skateboards were mostly flat, and the upturned kicktail later gave skaters a lever they could press.
reading: The first skateboards of the late 1950s were often homemade: a plank with roller-skate wheels nailed or bolted underneath. Store-made boards appeared around 1959. Companies such as Makaha, started by Larry Stevenson in 1963, and Hobie sold boards in the 1960s. Most of these early decks were flat from end to end.

On a flat board, the back end is still a lever, but it is hard to use. The tail sits low and flat, so it has little room to swing down before it touches the ground. Skaters of the 1960s did tricks such as handstands, walking the board and spinning on the back wheels. They did not do ollies.

Larry Stevenson was granted a U.S. patent for a *kicktail* in 1971. A kicktail is a tail that bends upward at the back of the deck. It gave the back foot a clear place to press and turned the end of the board into a handy lever. Today most decks turn up at both ends, with a kicked nose as well as a kicked tail.

words.d: a tail that bends upward at the back of the deck so the foot can press it like a lever
the flat board a skater stands on
a government record that names an inventor and protects an invention for a set time

look.title: Two Boards Side by Side
look.text: On the left of a table lies a 1960s-style board: flat from nose to tail, with the wheels near each end. On the right lies a modern deck: its tail and nose both curve upward, and the wheels sit a little farther in from the ends. Run a finger along each one from front to back.
look.prompt: Where would your back foot go on each board to tip the nose up? Which board gives the foot a clearer place to press, and why?

check.q: Who was granted a patent for the kicktail in 1971?
check.why: Larry Stevenson, who started Makaha in 1963, was granted the kicktail patent in 1971.

check.q: What shape were most skateboard decks in the early 1960s?
choices: Kicked up only at the nose
check.why: Most early decks were flat; the kicktail came later.

check.q: What is a kicktail?
choices: A wheel set at the back of the board
A tail that bends upward at the back of the deck
A kick that pushes the board forward
check.why: A kicktail is the upturned back end of the deck that the foot can press like a lever.

lessons.title: Why the Angle Helps
lessons.mainIdea: An upturned tail starts higher, so the board can turn farther before the tail hits the ground, and the foot finds it easily.
reading: Look at a board from the side. The deck rides a few centimeters above the ground on its trucks and wheels. On a flat board, the tail tip starts at that same low height. When the tail is pressed, the tip touches the ground after only a small turn. The nose cannot rise very high before the turning stops.

A kicktail bends upward, so its tip starts several centimeters higher. Pressed down, it has farther to travel before it meets the ground. That means the board turns through a bigger angle, and the nose climbs higher. The upturned shape also lets the tip strike the ground hard and fast, which makes the *pop*, the sharp crack that starts an ollie.

The angle helps the foot too. A skater can feel the bend under the shoe without looking down. That makes it easy to put the ball of the back foot in the same spot every time. Doing a move the same way again and again is how a skater builds *muscle memory*, the feel for a motion that comes from practice.

words.d: the sharp strike of the tail on the ground that starts an ollie, and the crack it makes
the feel for a motion that the body learns by repeating it many times

look.title: Measure the Swing
look.text: Lay a flat plank across a skateboard's trucks so it sticks out past the tail. Press the plank's end down until it touches the floor, and mark how high its front end rose. Now press the real kicked tail down until it touches the floor, and mark how high the nose rose. The kicked tail lets the front climb higher.
look.prompt: Explain the difference using the words pivot and angle. Why does a tail that starts higher let the nose rise higher?

check.q: Why can a kicked tail make the nose rise higher than a flat tail?
choices: Its tip starts higher, so the board turns farther before the tail touches
It moves the pivot to the front wheels
check.why: The raised tip has farther to travel down, so the board turns through a bigger angle.

check.q: What is the pop in an ollie?
choices: The front foot sliding up the board
The landing on all four wheels
The sharp strike of the tail on the ground
The sound of the wheels rolling
check.why: The pop is the tail tip striking the ground hard, with the crack that starts the ollie.

check.q: How does the bend of the kicktail help a skater build muscle memory?
choices: The foot can feel it and land in the same spot every time
It makes the skater look down
It removes the need to practice
check.why: Feeling the bend lets the foot find the same place each time, and repetition builds muscle memory.

lessons.title: Practicing the Pop Standing Still
lessons.mainIdea: A skater can learn the pop safely on grass or carpet, where the board cannot roll, before trying it while moving.
reading: Before practicing, buckle a helmet that fits snugly, wear flat shoes, and use wrist guards. Set the board on grass or a carpet so it cannot roll. Stand with the back foot's ball on the tail and the front foot just behind the front bolts. Both feet point across the board. Regular skaters have the left foot in front, and goofy skaters have the right foot in front. Both are normal.

First, bend your knees into a low crouch. Next, snap the back foot down hard on the tail, as if stomping a bug. At the same moment, start a small jump and let the front foot go light. The tail should tap the ground with a crack, and the nose should flick up. Then let the board settle and step back onto it over the bolts.

Two problems are common. If the nose barely lifts, your back foot is probably too close to the bolts, so slide it back toward the end of the tail. If the board shoots out in front of you, you are pushing the tail forward instead of straight down, so aim the stomp at the ground. Practice ten pops at a time, and rest when your legs feel tired.

words.d: riding with the left foot in front
riding with the right foot in front
a low stance with knees bent, ready to spring

look.title: One Pop, Step by Step
look.text: The board rests on grass. The back foot's ball sits on the tail tip, and the front foot sits just behind the front bolts. Knees bend. The back foot snaps down. Crack: the tail taps the grass. The nose flicks up toward the knees, then drops back down. The feet land back over the bolts.
look.prompt: Say the steps out loud in order as you picture them: crouch, snap, go light, land. Which step do you think is hardest, and how could you practice just that step?

check.q: Where does the back foot go to practice the pop?
choices: In the middle of the deck
With its ball on the tail
check.why: The ball of the back foot goes on the tail so the stomp has a long lever arm.

check.q: The board shoots out in front of you when you pop. What is the likely fix?
choices: Aim the stomp straight down at the ground
Move the front foot onto the nose
check.why: The board shoots forward when the tail is pushed forward instead of down, so aim the stomp at the ground.

check.q: Why practice the pop on grass or carpet first?
choices: The board cannot roll away there
check.why: Grass and carpet keep the board from rolling, so you can learn the motion before moving.

lessons.title: The Ground Pushes Back
lessons.mainIdea: When the tail strikes the ground, the ground pushes back up on the tail just as hard; that push is what pops the board.
reading: Push your palm against a wall. You can feel the wall pressing back on your hand. Isaac Newton described this in his book *Principia*, published in 1687. His third law of motion says that forces come in pairs. When one object pushes on a second object, the second pushes back on the first with an equal force in the opposite direction.

In an ollie, the tail tip slams down onto the ground. The tail pushes down on the ground. At that same instant, the ground pushes up on the tail with a force just as big. This upward push is called a *reaction force*. It lasts only a tiny moment, but it is large, because the tail hits fast and the hard ground does not give.

That quick upward shove at the very back of the board is the pop. It bounces the tail up off the ground and helps send the whole board upward. A soft surface, like thick grass, pushes back weakly because it squishes. That is why the pop sounds dull and feels weak on grass, and sharp on smooth concrete.

words.d: when one object pushes on another, the second pushes back with an equal force in the opposite direction
the push back from the second object in a pair of forces
Isaac Newton's 1687 book that set out his laws of motion

look.title: Newton's Third Law
look.text: Every action has an equal reaction pushing the opposite way. When two bodies act on each other, the forces they put on each other are always equal in size and point in opposite directions.
look.cite: Isaac Newton, Principia (1687), Law III, as given in Andrew Motte's English translation (1729), paraphrased
look.prompt: Name the two bodies acting on each other when the tail pops. Which way does each force point?

check.q: When the tail pushes down on the ground, what does the ground do?
choices: Nothing, because the ground cannot move
It pulls the tail down harder
It pushes up on the tail with an equal force
It pushes sideways on the wheels
check.why: By Newton's third law, the ground pushes back up on the tail with a force equal in size and opposite in direction.

check.q: In what year was Newton's Principia published?
check.why: Principia was published in 1687; Motte's English translation came in 1729.

check.q: Why is the pop weaker on thick grass than on concrete?
choices: Grass squishes, so it pushes back weakly
Grass moves the pivot to the nose
check.why: Soft grass gives way, so its push back on the tail is weaker than hard concrete's.

lessons.title: Getting Out of the Way
lessons.mainIdea: The skater must jump and pull the knees up so the board has room to rise; the board cannot lift a rider standing on it.
reading: A skateboard has no glue on its top. If a rider stays heavy and stiff on the deck, the board cannot rise, because the rider's weight pins it to the ground. So in an ollie the skater jumps. The jump starts almost at the same moment as the pop. The legs push the body up, then pull the knees toward the chest.

Pulling the knees up clears a space under the feet. The popped board rises into that space. Watched from the side, it looks as if the board is stuck to the shoes. Really, the board is flying up on its own, and the feet are staying just above it and guiding it.

This also explains a common problem. Some beginners pop the tail well but keep their legs straight. The nose comes up, then slams back down under their weight. The fix is to practice the jump on its own: crouch, spring up and tuck the knees high. Then add the pop. Falling is part of learning; if you lose the board, crouch low and roll instead of catching yourself with stiff, straight arms.

words.d: the pull of gravity on a body, found by mass × 9.8 m/s² near Earth's surface
pulling the knees up toward the chest in the air

look.title: Two Riders, One Pop
look.text: Rider A pops the tail and keeps both legs straight. The nose lifts a little, then smacks back down; the wheels never leave the ground. Rider B pops the tail and, at the same instant, springs up and tucks both knees. The board rises under Rider B's shoes, and both come down together.
look.prompt: What did Rider B do that Rider A did not? Practice the tuck jump without a board first, then describe how it feels.

check.q: Why can't the board rise if the rider stays stiff and heavy?
choices: The rider's weight pins the board to the ground
The wheels are glued to the ground
check.why: The board has nothing holding it to the feet, and a heavy rider's weight keeps it down.

check.q: What does tucking the knees do in an ollie?
choices: It clears space under the feet so the board can rise
check.why: Pulling the knees up leaves room for the popped board to rise beneath the feet.

check.q: If you lose the board during practice, what is the safer way to fall?
choices: Lock both arms straight to catch yourself
Jump as high as you can
check.why: Crouching low and rolling spreads out the fall; stiff straight arms are how wrists get hurt.

review.q: When a skater presses the tail, what part of the board acts as the fulcrum?
review.why: The board turns around the rear wheels, so they are the fulcrum.

review.q: What is the rule for torque?
review.why: Torque equals the force times its distance from the pivot, the lever arm.

review.q: A 300 N stomp lands 0.15 m from the rear wheels. What is the torque?
What does Newton's third law say happens when the tail hits the ground?
choices: The ground pushes back up on the tail with an equal force
The tail pushes harder than the ground
Gravity turns off for a moment
review.why: Forces come in equal, opposite pairs, so the ground pushes up on the tail as hard as the tail pushes down.

review.q: Why does a short drop of the tail make a big rise at the nose?
choices: The nose is lighter than the tail
The wheels push the nose up
The nose is much farther from the pivot
review.why: Points farther from the pivot move farther, and the nose is several times farther from the rear wheels than the tail tip.

review.q: In what year was Larry Stevenson granted the kicktail patent?
review.why: Stevenson founded Makaha in 1963 and was granted the kicktail patent in 1971.

review.q: What would happen if the front foot pressed hard at the moment of the pop?
choices: Its torque would fight the tail's torque, and the nose would stay down
review.why: The front foot makes a torque the other way; pressing hard can cancel the tail's torque.

review.q: Why must the skater jump during an ollie?
choices: To give the board room to rise under the feet
To move the pivot to the nose
To press the front foot down
review.why: The board cannot lift a heavy rider, so the skater jumps and tucks to clear space for it.

chapters.title: Friction, Timing and Hang Time
chapters.bigQuestion: How do friction, timing and gravity work together to carry a skater and board up and back down in about half a second?

story.title: One Hundred Eighteen Frames
story.kicker: A slow-motion video shows what eyes are too slow to see.
paragraphs: Jordan sets a phone on a backpack at the edge of the school's smooth, empty basketball court. The phone is set to record slow motion at 240 frames per second. That means it takes 240 pictures every second. Maya buckles her helmet, rolls slowly past the phone and does an ollie about 30 centimeters high, the length of a school ruler.

At normal speed the ollie is over in a blink. The board snaps up, Maya rises with it, and they come down together with a soft clack. Jordan says it looks like the board is stuck to her shoes. Maya laughs and says her feet are not glued to anything.

They sit on the bench and play the clip one frame at a time. First the tail hits the ground, and a tiny puff of dust jumps up. Then the nose rises. Then something surprising: the side of Maya's front shoe slides forward along the black grip tape, all the way up toward the nose. The board follows the shoe upward and tips level.

Jordan counts the frames from the moment the tail leaves the ground to the moment the wheels touch down again. The count is 118 frames. He divides 118 by 240 on his calculator and gets about 0.49 seconds. "Half a second," Maya says. "It feels a lot longer than that when I am up there."

On the last frames Maya's knees are bent deep, almost like she is sitting in a chair. Jordan asks why she lands like that. She shrugs and says it just feels softer. Their science teacher, reading over their shoulders, says that feeling has a reason, and so does every frame they just watched.
story.think: In the video, what made the board rise level instead of only tipping up at the nose?

lessons.title: What Grip Tape Does
lessons.mainIdea: Grip tape is a rough sheet on top of the deck that makes strong friction with a skater's shoes.
reading: Rub your fingertip across the top of a skateboard. It feels like coarse sandpaper. That rough layer is *grip tape*: a sheet covered in tiny, hard grains, with a sticky back that glues it to the deck. Most grip tape is black, and skaters often cut and file its edges to match the board's shape.

Grip tape is there for *friction*. Friction is a force that acts where two surfaces touch and resists them sliding past each other. The hard grains dig into the rubber sole of a shoe. That makes the shoe much harder to slide than it would be on smooth, painted wood.

There are two kinds of friction to know. The first, *static friction*, holds two surfaces still against each other, like a shoe planted while the skater rolls. Kinetic friction acts while surfaces are already sliding, like a shoe dragging along the board. Grip tape makes both kinds strong, so a foot can stay put, or it can pull the board along while it slides.

words.d: a rough, sandpaper-like sheet glued to the top of the deck so shoes do not slip
a force where two surfaces touch that resists them sliding past each other
friction that holds two touching surfaces still against each other
friction that acts while two surfaces are sliding past each other

look.title: Shoe on Wood, Shoe on Grip
look.text: Hold a sneaker sole-down on a smooth wooden shelf and push it sideways with one finger. It slides easily. Now set the same sneaker on a board's grip tape and push it the same way. It takes a much harder push to make it move, and you can hear the grains scratch the rubber as it goes.
look.prompt: Which kind of friction holds the shoe before it moves, and which kind acts once it is sliding? Try it and describe what you feel.

check.q: What is friction?
choices: A force that pulls objects toward Earth
A push from the ground after the tail strikes
The turning effect of a force
A force where surfaces touch that resists sliding
check.why: Friction acts where two surfaces touch and resists them sliding past each other.

check.q: Which kind of friction acts when a shoe is dragging along the grip tape?
check.why: Kinetic friction acts while two surfaces are already sliding past each other.

check.q: Why does a shoe slide less on grip tape than on smooth wood?
choices: The hard grains dig into the rubber sole
Grip tape makes the board heavier
check.why: The tiny hard grains bite into the rubber, which makes the friction much stronger.

lessons.title: The Front Foot Drags the Board
lessons.mainIdea: As the front shoe slides toward the nose, friction from the grip tape pulls the board up and forward with it.
reading: After the pop, the nose is pointing up and the back of the board is low. Now the front foot goes to work. The skater slides the outside edge of the front shoe, the little-toe side, forward along the grip tape toward the nose. This motion is called the *slide*, and it is what Maya's slow-motion video showed.

Friction always acts against the sliding between two surfaces. The shoe moves forward and up along the board, so friction on the board points forward and up too. The rough grip tape lets the shoe drag the board along with it. The board rises with the foot, and its back end lifts off the ground to follow.

Kinetic friction can be estimated with f = μN. Here f is the friction force, N is how hard the surfaces press together, and μ (the Greek letter mu) is the *coefficient of friction*, a number for how grippy the pair of surfaces is. As a worked example, say a rubber sole on grip tape has μ = 0.9, an example value, and the shoe presses in with 150 N. Then f = 0.9 × 150 N = 135 N of drag on the board.

words.d: in an ollie, dragging the side of the front shoe up the grip tape toward the nose
a number, written μ, that tells how grippy two surfaces are together
how hard two surfaces press straight into each other, written N in f = μN

look.title: The Slide in Frames
look.text: Frame 1: the tail has just cracked on the ground, and the nose is tipped up. Frame 10: the outside edge of the front shoe has slid a few centimeters forward. Frame 20: the shoe is nearly at the nose, and the back wheels have left the ground. Frame 30: the board is level under both feet.
look.prompt: In which direction does friction push on the board during these frames? What would happen if the grip tape were smooth?

check.q: Which part of the front shoe slides along the grip tape in an ollie?
choices: The outside edge, on the little-toe side
The bottom of the back shoe
check.why: The skater drags the outside edge of the front shoe, the little-toe side, up toward the nose.

check.q: A shoe presses into the grip tape with 150 N, and μ = 0.9 in this example. What is the friction force?
Why does the board rise along with the sliding front shoe?
choices: Friction on the board points the way the shoe slides, so it drags the board along
The front wheels push it up
The shoe is glued to the board
check.why: Friction acts against the sliding, so on the board it points forward and up with the shoe.

lessons.title: Leveling Out
lessons.mainIdea: At the top of the slide, the front foot pushes forward and a little down to bring the board level under both feet.
reading: If the board only tipped nose-up, it would fall back down tail-first. The slide fixes this. As the front shoe reaches the bend of the nose, the skater pushes it forward and slightly down. That push makes a torque that turns the nose down and lifts the tail. The board swings level, which skaters call *leveling out*.

Meanwhile, the back foot rises with the tucked knee. It stays lightly over the tail as the tail climbs. Now the board is flat in the air, with both feet just above it. This is the top of the ollie, the moment that looks like magic in photos.

Two problems show up here. If the board stays nose-up and lands on its tail, the front foot did not slide far enough, so drag it all the way to the bend of the nose. If the nose dips first and the board lands front wheels first, the front foot pushed down too early or too hard. Grip tape also matters: worn-smooth or wet grip loses its friction, so the slide cannot pull the board. Replace worn grip, and skate only when the ground is dry.

words.d: bringing the board flat in the air by pushing the front foot forward at the top of the slide
tilted so the front of the board is higher than the back

look.title: Two Endings
look.text: Ollie one: the front shoe stops halfway up the board. The board hangs nose-up and lands on its tail with a scrape. Ollie two: the front shoe drags all the way to the nose's bend, then pushes forward. The tail swings up, the board flattens, and all four wheels touch down at once.
look.prompt: What did the front foot do differently in ollie two? Act out both front-foot motions on a board resting on carpet.

check.q: What does the front foot do to level out the board?
choices: Lifts straight up off the board
Pushes forward and a little down at the nose's bend
check.why: At the top of the slide, pushing forward and slightly down turns the nose down and the tail up.

check.q: Your board keeps landing on its tail, nose-up. What is the likely fix?
choices: Pop harder with the front foot
Slide the front foot all the way to the bend of the nose
check.why: Landing nose-up means the slide stopped short; dragging the front foot to the nose levels the board.

check.q: Why does wet or worn grip tape make ollies harder?
choices: It loses friction, so the slide cannot drag the board
It makes the wheels spin faster
check.why: The slide works by friction; smooth or wet grip cannot pull the board up and forward.

lessons.title: Crouch and Pop
lessons.mainIdea: An ollie begins with a low crouch that stores up spring in the legs, then a sharp pop of the tail.
reading: An ollie has six parts in order: crouch, pop, slide, jump, level, land. Some of them overlap, but learning them in order helps. Before trying a rolling ollie, practice the whole motion standing still on grass or carpet. Wear a buckled helmet, flat shoes and wrist guards, and then move to smooth, dry, flat ground away from cars, rolling at a slow walking speed.

Step 1 is the crouch. With the ball of the back foot on the tail and the front foot just behind the front bolts, bend both knees deeply. Keep your shoulders over the board and in line with it, and look ahead. A deeper crouch lets the legs push for longer on the way up, so the jump has more power.

Step 2 is the pop. Snap the back foot straight down on the tail so the tip cracks against the ground. Think about a quick, hard snap, not a slow press. A fast strike makes a big, short reaction force from the ground. That is what bounces the tail up and starts the board rising.

words.d: how a skater stands on the board: where the feet go and how the body is set
an ollie done while the board is moving forward

look.title: The Coil Before the Spring
look.text: A skater rolls slowly across a smooth court. The back foot's ball rests on the tail. The front foot sits just behind the front bolts. Knees bend until the skater is low, like a spring pressed down. Shoulders stay square to the board, eyes forward. Then, in one quick motion, the back foot snaps down.
look.prompt: Crouch low with no board and spring straight up. Then crouch only a little and spring. Which one gets you higher, and why?

check.q: What are the six parts of an ollie, in order?
choices: Pop, crouch, jump, slide, land, level
Jump, pop, crouch, slide, level, land
Crouch, slide, pop, level, jump, land
Crouch, pop, slide, jump, level, land
check.why: The order is crouch, pop, slide, jump, level, land.

check.q: Why does a deeper crouch help the ollie?
choices: The legs can push for longer on the way up
It keeps the tail from touching the ground
check.why: Bending lower gives the legs more distance to push through, which powers the jump.

check.q: What kind of motion makes a good pop?
choices: A slow press on the front bolts
A gentle push forward on the tail
A quick, hard snap straight down on the tail
check.why: A fast snap down makes a large, short push back from the ground that bounces the tail up.

lessons.title: Slide and Jump
lessons.mainIdea: Right after the pop, the front foot slides toward the nose while the skater jumps and tucks, almost all at once.
reading: Step 3 is the slide. As soon as the tail cracks, the front shoe starts dragging forward along the grip tape. The outside edge of the shoe leads the way toward the nose. Your slow-motion video, if you film one, will show the slide starting just a few frames after the pop.

Step 4 is the jump. In real time it happens almost together with the pop and slide. Spring up out of the crouch and pull both knees toward your chest. The back foot rises with the climbing tail. The front foot keeps sliding as the knees come up. The pop, the slide and the jump overlap, and that is why they feel like one move once you know them.

A useful drill is to practice these steps with the board still on carpet or grass. Say each word aloud as you do it: pop, slide, jump. Start slow and small. When the order feels natural, try it rolling slowly. Feeling nervous before your first rolling ollie is normal. It is your body asking you to take smaller steps, so go back to standing still whenever you need to.

words.d: when two steps happen partly at the same time
a short practice of one part of a skill, repeated

look.title: Three Moves in One Breath
look.text: Crack goes the tail. In the very next instant, the front shoe begins to slide up the grip. The skater's knees lift toward the chest. The back foot floats up off the rising tail. The board climbs between the feet. From start to finish, these three moves take less time than it takes to say them.
look.prompt: Clap once for the pop, swish your hand forward for the slide, and lift your knees for the jump. Now do all three faster and closer together. What changes?

check.q: When does the jump happen in an ollie?
choices: Almost at the same moment as the pop and slide
Long after the board levels out
check.why: In real time the jump overlaps with the pop and the slide.

check.q: What does the back foot do during the jump?
choices: It rises with the climbing tail
It stays pressed on the tail
check.why: As the knees tuck, the back foot lifts and rides up with the tail.

check.q: What does nervousness before a rolling ollie tell you?
choices: That you should take smaller steps, like practicing standing still
check.why: Fear is a normal signal; going back to smaller steps, like standing-still practice, helps.

lessons.title: Level and Land
lessons.mainIdea: The front foot levels the board, then both feet come down over the bolts with bent knees.
reading: Step 5 is the level. At the top of the jump the front foot pushes forward at the nose, and the board flattens under both feet. The skater keeps the knees tucked and the eyes on the board's bolts. This is the highest point of the ollie.

Step 6 is the land. Gravity brings the skater and board back down together. Set both feet down over the bolts, not on the tail or the nose. Feet over the bolts press straight down on the trucks, so the board stays level and rolls away smoothly. Bend your knees deeply as the wheels touch, and keep your shoulders over the board.

Many first landings end with a foot off the board. That is normal. If you are falling, step off, crouch low and let your knee pads take the slide, or roll onto your side. Do not reach out with straight arms. Each try teaches the feet a bit more about where the board will be, so the landings get steadier with practice.

words.d: to come back down onto the board with both feet
the metal parts under the deck that hold the wheels and let the board turn

look.title: Where the Feet Come Down
look.text: Picture the deck from above with two bolt patterns of four bolts each, one near each end. The back foot lands across the rear bolts and the front foot lands across the front bolts. Now picture a landing with the back foot on the tail tip: the tail tips down, the nose pops up, and the board shoots out.
look.prompt: Why does landing over the bolts keep the board steady? Use the word pivot in your answer.

check.q: Where should both feet land after an ollie?
choices: In the very middle, side by side
check.why: Feet over the bolts press straight down on the trucks, so the board stays level.

check.q: What brings the skater and board back down?
check.why: Gravity pulls the skater and board back toward the ground.

check.q: Which is a safe way to fall when a landing goes wrong?
choices: Catch yourself with straight, locked arms
Lean back and sit on the tail
Crouch low and slide on your knee pads or roll
check.why: Crouching, sliding on pads or rolling spreads out the fall; straight arms put the wrists at risk.

lessons.title: The Center of Mass
lessons.mainIdea: A body's center of mass is its balance point, and in the air it follows a path that arms and legs cannot change.
reading: Balance a ruler on one finger. There is one spot where it stays level. That spot is the ruler's *center of mass*, the point where its mass acts as if it were all gathered together. A standing person's center of mass is usually inside the body, a little below the belly button.

When a skater crouches, the center of mass drops lower. When the skater springs up, it rises. Once the skater and board leave the ground, gravity is the main force acting on them. From that moment, the path of the center of mass is set. Waving the arms or tucking the knees cannot make it go higher or come down later.

Tucking still matters, though. Pulling the knees up raises the feet closer to the center of mass. So the feet and board rise more than the center of mass does. A skater whose center of mass rises 30 cm can lift the board even higher by tucking well. That is why good ollies look so tall.

words.d: the balance point of an object, where its mass acts as if it were all gathered
the pull of Earth that makes things fall, speeding them up by 9.8 m/s every second

look.title: Two Jumps, Same Center
look.text: Two jumpers spring up with the same push. One keeps the legs straight. The other tucks the knees to the chest. Their centers of mass rise the same height and land at the same moment. But the tucked jumper's feet get much higher off the ground, because the feet moved up toward the middle of the body.
look.prompt: Try a straight jump and a tuck jump. In which jump did your feet get higher? Did you stay in the air longer?

check.q: What is the center of mass?
choices: The heaviest part of the board
The point where the tail strikes
The balance point where an object's mass acts as if gathered
The middle of the grip tape
check.why: The center of mass is the balance point of an object.

check.q: Once a skater is in the air, can waving the arms make the center of mass go higher?
choices: Yes, if the arms wave fast
No, its path is set once the skater leaves the ground
Yes, if the knees stay straight
check.why: In the air, gravity sets the path of the center of mass; moving limbs cannot change it.

check.q: Why can the board rise higher than the skater's center of mass?
choices: Tucking pulls the feet up toward the center of mass
The board is lighter than air
check.why: Tucking lifts the feet closer to the center of mass, so the feet and board climb farther.

lessons.title: A Curve Called a Parabola
lessons.mainIdea: In the air the center of mass rises, slows, stops at the top and falls along a curve called a parabola.
reading: Toss a ball gently forward and watch its path. It climbs, curves over the top and comes back down in a smooth arch. That shape is a *parabola*. Any object moving freely through the air, with gravity as the only big force, follows a parabola. A skater's center of mass does too during an ollie.

Gravity changes the up-and-down speed by 9.8 m/s every second. On the way up, the skater slows down until, at the top, the up-and-down speed is zero for an instant. That top point is the *peak*. On the way down, the skater speeds up again. The trip down mirrors the trip up, so the rise and the fall take the same time.

Here is a worked example. A skater leaves the ground moving upward at about 2.4 m/s. Height after time t is 2.4t − 4.9t², in meters. After 0.10 s: 2.4 × 0.10 − 4.9 × 0.01 = 0.24 − 0.049 ≈ 0.19 m. After 0.25 s: 0.60 − 0.306 ≈ 0.29 m, which is the peak. With the speed rounded to 2.4 m/s, the peak lands just under 0.30 m. The table shows the full curve.

words.d: the smooth arch-shaped path of an object moving freely under gravity
the highest point of a jump, where the up-and-down speed is zero for an instant

look.title: Height of the Center of Mass Over Time
look.cite: Worked example with g = 9.8 m/s², upward launch speed about 2.4 m/s
look.prompt: Find two times with the same height, one going up and one coming down. What does this tell you about the shape of the path?

check.q: What is the shape of the path of a skater's center of mass in an ollie?
choices: A straight line up and down
check.why: Anything moving freely with gravity as the only big force follows a parabola.

check.q: What is true of the up-and-down speed at the peak?
choices: It is the fastest of the whole jump
It is zero for an instant
It is the same as the forward speed
check.why: At the peak the skater has stopped rising and not yet started falling, so the up-and-down speed is zero.

check.q: In the worked example, about how high is the center of mass after 0.10 s?

lessons.title: Why the Board Stays Under You
lessons.mainIdea: The skater and board keep the same forward speed in the air, so a rolling ollie lands back on the board.
reading: In a rolling ollie the board and skater are moving forward before the pop. Newton's first law says an object keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction unless a force changes it. That tendency to keep moving is called *inertia*. In the air, nothing pushes the skater or board forward or backward much, so both keep their forward speed.

That is why the board stays under the feet. The skater and board started with the same forward speed, and they keep it together. Here is a worked example. If they roll at 3 m/s, an example speed, and stay in the air 0.49 s, they both travel 3 × 0.49 ≈ 1.5 m forward. They land together, about 1.5 m down the court.

Put the up-and-down motion together with the steady forward motion, and you get the parabola. The forward part stays the same, and the up-and-down part rises and falls. Air pushes back a little on both, but at slow skating speeds that push is small. A skater who leans back or pushes the tail forward during the pop changes the board's speed, and the board rolls away ahead.

words.d: the tendency of an object to keep moving the same way, or stay still, unless a force acts
an object keeps its speed and direction unless an outside force changes it

look.title: Newton's First Law
look.text: Every body keeps doing what it is doing, staying at rest or moving straight ahead at a steady speed, unless forces acting on it make it change.
look.cite: Isaac Newton, Principia (1687), Law I, as given in Andrew Motte's English translation (1729), paraphrased
look.prompt: Which force changes the skater's up-and-down motion in the air? Why does the forward motion stay nearly the same?

check.q: What is inertia?
choices: The pull of Earth on an object
The friction between shoe and grip
The tendency of an object to keep moving the same way unless a force acts
The push from the ground at the pop
check.why: Inertia is the tendency to keep the same motion unless a force changes it.

check.q: A skater rolls at 3 m/s and stays in the air 0.49 s. About how far forward does the skater travel?
check.why: Distance = speed × time = 3 × 0.49 ≈ 1.5 m.

check.q: Why does a rolling ollie land back on the board?
choices: The skater and board keep the same forward speed
The board is pulled toward the feet by friction
The wheels steer under the feet
check.why: By inertia, both keep the forward speed they shared before the pop.

lessons.title: Higher Jumps, Longer Hang Time
lessons.mainIdea: Hang time grows with jump height, but slowly: four times the height gives only twice the time.
reading: A skater's *hang time* is how long a skater stays in the air during a jump. It depends only on how high the center of mass rises. For a jump that rises a height h and lands at the same level, hang time = 2√(2h ÷ g), where g = 9.8 m/s². The 2 out front is there because the trip down takes as long as the trip up.

The table shows worked results for five heights. Notice how hang time grows. Going from 0.10 m to 0.40 m is four times as high, but the time only goes from 0.29 s to 0.57 s, about twice as long. That happens because of the *square root*. Gravity speeds up a falling object every moment, so each extra centimeter of height adds less extra time.

This is why even big ollies are short. A very high ollie of 0.50 m gives about 0.64 s in the air. Pros look as if they float, partly because tucking lifts the board higher than the center of mass. But physics keeps every flat-ground ollie well under one second.

lessons.title: Working Out a 30 cm Ollie
lessons.mainIdea: A 30 cm ollie keeps a rider in the air about half a second, which matches the slow-motion frame count.
reading: Let's work out the hang time of a 30 cm ollie step by step. First change centimeters to meters: 30 cm = 0.30 m. Next find 2h: 2 × 0.30 = 0.60. Then divide by g: 0.60 ÷ 9.8 ≈ 0.0612. The square root of 0.0612 is about 0.247. That is the time to rise, in seconds.

Finally, double it for the trip down: 2 × 0.247 ≈ 0.49 s. So a rider whose center of mass rises 30 cm stays in the air about half a second. About 0.25 s goes to rising and about 0.25 s goes to falling.

This matches the story's video. At 240 *frames per second*, 0.49 s fills 0.49 × 240 ≈ 118 frames. The frame count, 118 ÷ 240 ≈ 0.49 s, and the hang time rule give the same answer. Checking a calculation against a real measurement like this is how scientists test whether a rule works.

lessons.title: Bend Your Knees
lessons.mainIdea: Bending the knees on landing stretches out the stopping time, which makes the force on the body much smaller.
reading: Jump off a low step and land with stiff legs, and you feel a jolt. Land with bent knees, and it feels soft. The difference is time. To stop a falling body, a force has to take away its downward speed. If the stopping happens quickly, the force must be large. If it takes longer, the force can be small.

From a 0.30 m rise, a skater comes down at about √(2 × 9.8 × 0.30) = √5.88 ≈ 2.4 m/s. Take a 50 kg skater as a worked example. Stiff legs might stop the fall in 0.05 s. The slowing is 2.4 ÷ 0.05 = 48 m/s², so by F = ma the force is 50 × 48 = 2,400 N. Bent knees might stretch the stop to 0.25 s: 2.4 ÷ 0.25 = 9.6 m/s², and 50 × 9.6 = 480 N.

These are the extra forces needed to stop the fall, on top of the skater's own weight. Bending the knees cut the force to one fifth, because the stop took five times as long. This is the same idea behind knee pads, helmets and the soft foam inside them: each one makes a hit last longer, so the force is smaller. To *absorb* a landing means to spread it out over time.

words.d: to soak up a hit by spreading it over a longer time, so the force is smaller
